planting.note: Set bare-root crowns in early spring at soil level in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; choose a site with good air movement, since this older cultivar is more disease-prone than modern releases.

directions: Fairfax was released by the USDA strawberry breeding program in the early 1930s under breeder George M. Darrow and is still cited today chiefly for its intense, aromatic flavor, long considered one of the benchmarks against which later dessert-type strawberries were judged. The medium-sized, deep red berries are soft and bruise easily, so the plant never suited commercial shipping and has largely disappeared from retail nurseries, surviving mainly in germplasm collections, breeding programs, and home gardens of flavor-focused growers. It is also more susceptible to red stele root rot and other soil-borne diseases than many modern cultivars, so plant in well-drained soil free of prior strawberry or bramble crops. Because of its outstanding flavor, Fairfax has been used repeatedly as breeding stock in later mid-20th-century American strawberry breeding programs.
